core: Verification versus validation as two different questions, stated from both a systems-engineering source and the metrology vocabulary
The four verification methods - inspection, analysis, demonstration, test - and the conditions that select each
Bidirectional requirements traceability, and why a requirement that cannot be verified is defective rather than merely vague
Test planning: objective, configuration, procedure and acceptance criteria with tolerances fixed before the run, and why a criterion chosen afterward destroys the evidentiary value of the test
Instrumentation, measurement uncertainty as a required part of any reported result, and metrological traceability through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations

Introductory design of experiments: factors, levels, responses, controlled and uncontrolled variables, replication, randomization, blocking, one-factor-at-a-time versus full factorial, and interactions
Destructive testing versus non-destructive evaluation, and probability of detection as the honest statement of NDE capability
Accelerated life testing, the acceleration factor, and the assumption that the accelerated failure mechanism is the field failure mechanism
Verification, qualification, acceptance and certification as distinct programmes; environmental testing at the extremes of the envelope

Statistical treatment: sample mean, standard deviation, t-based confidence interval for the mean, what such an interval does and does not mean, and why one passing unit cannot support a population claim
Failure analysis: direct cause, contributing cause and root cause; regression testing after a corrective change
supporting: Censoring and lack of failures as the structural difficulty of reliability testing
Fractional factorial and Plackett-Burman designs, named only as the answer to run-count growth
outOfScope: The design loop itself and the first introduction of V and V in context - owned by engineering-design-process
Prototype types and fidelity levels - owned by prototyping
Factors of safety and failure theories - owned by safety-factors-and-failure

Foundational treatment of SI units, significant figures, precision/trueness/accuracy and the Type A/Type B uncertainty framework - owned by units-measurement-and-significant-figures and only referenced here
Specific test levels, durations, acceptance limits, flaw sizes or sampling plans from any standard
Hypothesis-testing machinery beyond the confidence interval for a mean
Software test taxonomies (unit, integration, system) beyond regression testing

claims.claim: NASA/SP-2016-6105 Rev2 defines verification as a formal process, using the method of test, analysis, inspection or demonstration, to confirm that a system and its associated hardware and software components satisfy all specified requirements, and states that the verification programme is performed once regardless of how many flight units are generated as long as the design does not change. Validation shows that the product accomplishes the intended purpose in the intended environment and meets stakeholder expectations. The handbook frames the pair as the questions 'Was the end product realized right?' and 'Was the right end product realized?' Verification traces to the approved requirements set; validation traces to the ConOps.

JCGM 200:2012 (VIM) 2.44 defines verification as provision of objective evidence that a given item fulfils specified requirements, and 2.45 defines validation as verification where the specified requirements are adequate for an intended use. VIM 2.44 Note 5 states that not every verification is a validation. The VIM formulation therefore makes validation an extension of verification rather than a parallel activity.

NASA names four methods of verification. Analysis: mathematical modelling and analytical techniques, generally used when a prototype, engineering model or fabricated product is not available, including modelling, simulation and verification by similarity to a heritage product. Demonstration: showing that use of an end product achieves the specified requirement, generally a basic confirmation of performance capability differentiated from testing by the lack of detailed data gathering. Inspection: visual examination of a realized end product, generally used for physical design features or manufacturer identification, and able to include inspection of drawings, documents or records. Test: use of an end product to obtain detailed data at discrete points under controlled conditions, and the most resource-intensive verification technique, accompanied by the maxim 'Test as you fly, and fly as you test.'

NASA states that all requirements should be verifiable, meaning stated in a fashion and with enough information that it will be possible to verify the requirement after the end product is implemented, and its requirements checklist asks whether requirements are free of unverifiable terms, listing flexible, easy, sufficient, safe, ad hoc, adequate, accommodate, user-friendly, usable, appropriate, fast, robust, quickly, easily, clearly, other words ending in -ly and other words ending in -ize.

NASA requires that each requirement's bidirectional traceability be recorded: traced back to a parent or source requirement in a baselined document, or identified as self-derived with concurrence sought. If there is no parent and the requirement is not an acceptable self-derived requirement, it should be assumed either that the traceability process is flawed and should be redone or that the requirement is gold plating and should be eliminated. Traceability is usually recorded in a requirements matrix or a requirements modelling application.

NASA's example of the information in a verification procedure - written before the run - includes identification of the test article, identification of the test configuration and any differences from the flight operational configuration, identification of objectives and criteria established for the verification by the applicable requirements specification, the characteristics and design criteria to be inspected, demonstrated or tested including values with tolerances for acceptance or rejection, a description in sequence of the steps, operations and observations to be taken, and identification of measuring, test and recording equipment specifying range, accuracy and type, with provision for recording equipment calibration or software version data.

NIST describes the statistical design of experiments as an efficient procedure for planning experiments so that the data obtained can be analysed to yield valid and objective conclusions, and defines an experimental design as the laying out of a detailed experimental plan in advance of doing the experiment. Its black-box process model distinguishes controllable input factors, measured output responses, and uncontrolled factors that may be discrete (different machines or operators) or continuous (ambient temperature, humidity). Its linear model includes an X1X2 term to account for a possible interaction effect, and for three factors names three main-effect terms, k(k-1)/2 = 3 two-way interaction terms and one three-way interaction term.

The NIST DOE glossary defines an interaction as occurring when the effect of one factor on a response depends on the level of another factor; replication as performing the same treatment combination more than once, which allows random error to be estimated; randomization as a schedule for allocating material and conducting runs such that conditions in one run neither depend on previous conditions nor predict subsequent ones; and blocking as a schedule under which the effects of known nuisance changes such as different operators or machines become concentrated in the levels of the blocking variable, achieved by restricting randomization.

A two-level full factorial design with k factors has 2^k runs; NIST's table gives 4 runs for 2 factors, 8 for 3, 16 for 4, 32 for 5, 64 for 6 and 128 for 7, and NIST states that with 5 or more factors a full factorial is not very efficient and that a fractional factorial or Plackett-Burman design is a better choice.

From a 2^3 full factorial, seven effects can be estimated - three main effects, three two-factor interactions and one three-factor interaction, since C(3,1)+C(3,2)+C(3,3) = 3+3+1 = 7 - while a one-factor-at-a-time sweep of the same three factors from a baseline uses four runs (baseline plus one change per factor) and contains no run in which two factors move together, so no interaction term can be estimated from it. Run counts and effect counts were computed in Python.

VIM 2.41 defines metrological traceability as the property of a measurement result whereby the result can be related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the measurement uncertainty; Note 2 states that it requires an established calibration hierarchy, and Note 5 states that metrological traceability of a measurement result does not ensure that the measurement uncertainty is adequate for a given purpose or that there is an absence of mistakes.

NIST defines an unbroken chain of calibrations as a complete, explicitly described and documented series of calibrations that successively link a measurement result (measured value and associated uncertainty) to the values and uncertainties of each intermediate reference standard and to the highest reference standard to which traceability is claimed. NIST policy further states that supporting a claim of metrological traceability is the responsibility of the provider of the result and assessing the validity of the claim is the responsibility of the user, that traceability is a property of a measurement result and not of an institution, and that traceability alone does not guarantee fitness for purpose.

Uncertainty components are evaluated as Type A (statistical analysis of a series of observations) or Type B (other means, including calibration certificates, manufacturer specifications and handbook values), combined into a combined standard uncertainty uc, and expanded as U = k*uc; NIST states that k is generally chosen for the desired level of confidence, that k = 2 defines an interval with a level of confidence of approximately 95 percent and k = 3 a level of confidence greater than 99 percent, when uc is a reliable estimate of the standard deviation of the result.

NASA-STD-5009C defines nondestructive evaluation as the development and application of technical methods to examine materials or components in ways that do not impair future usefulness and serviceability, to detect, locate, measure and evaluate flaws and to assess integrity, properties and composition.

NASA-STD-5009C requirement NER 2 states that nondestructive inspections of fracture-critical hardware shall detect the initial crack sizes used in the damage tolerance fracture analyses with a capability of minimum 90 percent probability of detection at a 95 percent confidence level, known as 90/95, and defines the reliably detectable flaw size, which is assumed to exist in a part for the purpose of performing the damage-tolerance safe-life analysis. No flaw sizes or tables from the standard are reproduced in this lesson.

NIST states that physical (true) acceleration means that operating a unit at high stress produces the same failures that would occur at typical-use stresses, except much sooner, from the same causes on a different time scale; the acceleration factor AF is the constant multiplier between the two stress levels, with time to fail at use equal to AF times time to fail at stress. NIST notes that different failure modes are affected differently by stress and have different acceleration factors, so it is unlikely a single acceleration factor applies to more than one failure mechanism, and failure data should be separated by failure mode.

NIST names censoring (when the observation period ends, not all units have failed) and lack of failures (too much censoring leaves limited information even with many units under observation) as the two characteristic difficulties of reliability data, and states the paradox that the more reliable a product is, the harder it is to get the failure data needed to prove it is reliable.

NASA distinguishes verification, qualification, acceptance and certification: the verification programme is performed once for a design as long as the design does not change; qualification performs a subset of the verification programme at the extremes of the environmental envelope to ensure the design operates with expected margins, and is performed once regardless of how many flight units are generated; acceptance is a smaller subset performed on each flight unit as manufactured, selected to show that manufacturing and workmanship conform to the previously verified and qualified design; certification is the audit process by which the body of evidence is provided to the appropriate certifying authority. NASA also notes that validation testing focuses on expected environments and operations whereas qualification testing includes worst-case loads and environments.

NIST gives the two-sided confidence interval for a mean with unknown standard deviation as the sample mean plus and minus (s/sqrt(N)) times the t critical value at N-1 degrees of freedom, and states that confidence intervals are constructed so that the probability of the interval containing the mean is 1 - alpha. Its worked example uses t(0.975, 9) = 2.262.

For the ten illustrative (synthetic) measurements 11.42, 12.05, 11.78, 12.34, 11.61, 12.11, 11.95, 12.48, 11.70 and 12.02 N: sample mean 11.946 N, sample standard deviation 0.3268 N, standard error 0.1033 N, t(0.975, 9) = 2.2622, half-width 0.2338 N, and 95 percent confidence interval for the mean 11.71 N to 12.18 N. Holding the same scatter, the smallest N giving a half-width no greater than 0.10 N is 44. All values were computed in Python; the t-quantile routine was written from the regularized incomplete beta function and validated against published values t(0.975,1) = 12.706, t(0.975,9) = 2.262, t(0.95,10) = 1.812 and t(0.975,29) = 2.045.

With zero failures in n independent trials, the one-sided 95 percent upper confidence bound on the population failure fraction is 1 - 0.05^(1/n): 95.0 percent for n = 1, 25.9 percent for n = 10 and 9.50 percent for n = 30, the last matching the rule-of-three approximation 3/30 = 10 percent. Each bound was checked in Python by confirming that (1 - bound)^n = 0.05. A single passing unit therefore supports no useful claim about the population.

DOE-NE-STD-1004-92 defines the direct cause as the cause that directly resulted in the occurrence; a contributing cause as a cause that contributed to an occurrence but by itself would not have caused the occurrence; and the root cause as the cause that, if corrected, would prevent recurrence of this and similar occurrences, noting that the root cause has generic implications to a broad group of possible occurrences, is the most fundamental aspect of the cause that can logically be identified and corrected, and is reached by pursuing a series of causes until the fundamental correctable cause has been identified.

NASA states that when reengineering a deficient end product, care should be taken that correcting a deficiency does not generate a new issue with a part or performance that had previously operated satisfactorily, and names regression testing - a formal process of rerunning previously used acceptance tests, primarily used for software - as one method to ensure a change does not affect function or performance that was previously accepted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How verification and validation are worded differs between systems engineering and metrology.
positions: NASA frames the pair operationally: verification confirms compliance with specified requirements by test, analysis, inspection or demonstration; validation confirms the product accomplishes its intended purpose in the intended environment.

The VIM frames the pair definitionally: verification is objective evidence that an item fulfils specified requirements, and validation is verification where the specified requirements are adequate for an intended use.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a conflict but two levels of abstraction that agree. The lesson gives the VIM wording as the compact logical statement and the NASA wording as the programme-level one, and notes that the VIM formulation makes validation an extension of verification rather than a parallel activity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether regression testing is a software-only practice.
positions: NASA's handbook describes regression testing as a formal process of rerunning previously used acceptance tests, primarily used for software.
The concern it addresses - that a fix can break something that previously worked - is stated by NASA in general product terms, not software terms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the practice as NASA states it, naming its primary use in software, while teaching the general principle that any change reopens previously closed verification, which is what the handbook's reengineering caution actually says.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether one-factor-at-a-time experimentation is criticised by the cited sources.
positions: The NIST handbook pages read for this lesson do not name or criticise one-factor-at-a-time experimentation.
The same pages define interactions as effects that appear only when factor levels are combined, and show that a factorial layout carries interaction terms.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson derives the OFAT limitation from the sourced definitions rather than attributing a criticism to NIST: an OFAT sweep contains no run in which two factors move together, so it holds no data from which an interaction term could be estimated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly NIST's traceability page can be cited for the requirements of a traceability claim.
positions: An earlier unverified draft of this topic stated that NIST requires three specific elements for a traceability claim, including a description of the measurement process.

Direct reading of the NIST page supports the unbroken documented chain with uncertainty at every step, the provider's responsibility for supporting the claim, and traceability being a property of a result rather than of an institution, but does not state that three-element formulation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The claim was rewritten to exactly what the page states, and the lesson prose was corrected to match. Nothing in the lesson now attributes the three-element formulation to NIST.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-1/lessons.json contained no factual content about testing or validation: its In 30 Seconds, Why This Matters, College Version, vocabulary, worked example, mistakes and questions were topic-agnostic boilerplate that would fit any lesson in any subject.
That draft defined 'Testing And Validation' circularly as a foundational Engineering Fundamentals concept covered in this lesson.
That draft's analogy carried no engineering content and had no analogyLimits.

Every source URL, definition and number in that draft was re-fetched and re-executed in this run before any of it was carried forward; one claim (the NIST three-element traceability formulation) did not survive re-verification and was corrected.
correctionsNeeded: Rewrote the topic from the verification-versus-validation distinction, replacing the generated boilerplate entirely.

Corrected the NIST metrological-traceability claim: the previous draft's three-element formulation is not what the NIST page states. Replaced with NIST's definition of an unbroken chain, the provider/user responsibility split, and the point that traceability is a property of a result rather than of an institution.
Restated the acceleration factor in NIST's own form (time to fail at use equals AF times time to fail at stress) rather than as an unverified ratio of model functions.
Added the four NASA verification methods with their defining conditions, which the generated draft did not mention.

Added a fully executed worked example: mean, standard deviation, t-based 95 percent confidence interval, the sample size needed for a tighter interval, and the zero-failure binomial upper bound showing that one passing unit supports no population claim.
Added the educational-material and not-engineering-design-guidance statements required for this subject.

DOE-NE-STD-1004-92 is a U.S. Department of Energy guideline in the public domain; its cause definitions were restated in original wording.

NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook pages, the NIST CUU uncertainty pages and the NIST metrological traceability page carry no explicit reuse licence and are treated REFERENCE_ONLY; facts were synthesized and rewritten.
